title: Salsa Fargo 32 Steel Review: 32 Coming Through – Sean T. Randolph & Spencer Harding
content:
“32 Coming through!” Sean yelled at his friends as he passed them, going downhill on Harshaw Road. Why is he passing his friends all of a sudden? Is it bigger wheels? Is 32” faster? Or is he just boasting because he’s riding the new monster truck of drop bar MTB’s, the Salsa Fargo 32? Read on to see what’s going on with the new steel Fargo 32” and if it does indeed go far, then how far does it go…

For a very long time, my favorite bicycle was a 2008 Salsa Ala Carte in Goldrush Brown. You can see a picture of the bike in Salsa’s archive if you look up 2010 Salsa Ala Carte. This 26” MTB went everywhere with me and withstood many upgrades and Iterations: rim brake to disc, tubes to tubeless, 8 to 9 to 10 speed, and so on. The model was one of the few that held over from the original Ross Schafer days. If you don’t know about Ross, I recommend checking him out.

This bike was very important to me for many reasons, but it established how a quality bike should feel. It had True Temper Ox platinum tubing, which made the frame hella flexy, but oh so comfortable. The 26” wheels were stiff and nimble, and I was used to them, so I held out from getting a 29er way past when it was acceptable. You know those stickers that say “26 ain’t dead yet,” well, that was my mantra.

I have since moved on but hold a little bit of that “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” attitude. Naturally, my entry into the 32” world was laced with a healthy dose of skepticism, and at the same time riding the Steel Fargo 32” gave me feelings of riding my own Salsa relic.

Salsa Fargo 32 Steel Frameset Quick Hits

  • Small, Medium, Large, X-Large sizing
  • Pearl Orchid paint
  • Standard boost spacing
  • Internal dropper routing
  • Internal dynamo wire routing on carbon fork
  • Front and rear rack mounting options, as well as anything cage mounts on the frame and fork
  • Triple-butted chromoly tubeset
  • Alternator 1.0 flat-mount dropouts with UDH accommodate Transmission drivetrains and belt drive systems
  • Alternator dropouts are available for flat or post-mount brakes
  • Fork is post-mount and will need a Wolftooth post-flat adaptor for drop bar groups
  • Multi-fit geometry that accommodates both flat and drop bar setups
  • Steel Frameset is listed for $1799 USD (frame, fork, headset, thru axles, and seat collar)
  • Also available in Ti for $3499

The Steel Fargo 32” is currently only offered as a frameset and comes in one striking color: Pearl Orchid. I love flashy bikes. Pearly paint jobs and metallic glitter, yes please! Take me back to the days of Schwinn Homegrown bass boat paint and the pink 2 Hip Pork. The Fargo’s paint morphs between lilac purple and sage green depending on the light. It also has a shimmery metallic flake. If you have read any of my other reviews, you know that I’m big on subtle logos and branding. The Salsa logos on the downtube are bold, but match the green sheen of the paint nicely, so they get an aesthetic pass. But how does it ride, you ask? Well, I’d argue that a good part of what makes a bike ride well is how you feel on the bike. When I buy a skateboard, I do care about the artwork. It’s true that I’m going to scrape the bottom paint off on my first boardslide, but it has to feel right. Same with the Salsa frame, it’s gonna get covered in dirt (and it did; we got stuck in a monsoon) and bags, but you want the frame to look good underneath it all. We often forget this, but I’d like to remind you that the way things look matters. And this bike does look good. The build we reviewed came with silver wheels, tan wall tires, and black components. Very classy.

Does The Fargo 32 Shred?

But Sean, does the bike shred? The short answer is, yes, it does shred. If I were to make an even more complete review of this bike, I would have a size run and try every size with every size rider, but I do not have this luxury, so we’ll have to settle for someone 6 feet tall (me) and someone else 6 feet 1 inch (Spencer) riding an XL frame. The XL frame fit me well, but was on the big side. I think I’d prefer the Large for my own bike. Salsa equipped the bike with a 70mm -25 degree stem that the bike was designed around. This accommodates the 80mm suspension-corrected fork and 32” wheel. It looks a little funny at first, but I can assure you that it doesn’t handle funny. The bike is stable and slack, but responsive at speed. The stem drop made me think someone much taller than me could ride the bike with a positive-rise stem and have a very happy back.

My question is then, why doesn’t the bike come in an XXL? This seems like an instance where bigger wheels mean the bike should follow suit. This is not an original idea, but it seems like something we might see in the land of 32” as a design choice to accommodate taller riders. Salsa responded with two reasons: firstly, the economics of producing a niche size. Second, their multi-fit geo should accommodate much larger riders with a longer stem.

One of my main concerns about the bike was that the larger wheels would mean excess flex. To be clear, I am a fan of flex, but too much can lead to a sloppy ride. The bike came with silver i9 hubs laced to silver Velocity Blunt SS rims. Out of the box, the wheels didn’t feel too tankish, and on the bike they felt smooth as buttah’. While standing out of the saddle, they were peppy and maintained a good line downhill. The best way to describe the ride feel of a 32” wheel with a 2.4 tire is “comfortable.” I know that’s not the most exciting word to describe a bike, but outside of how a bike looks, comfort is king. On a bike like this, comfort means you can ride longer, harder, and stronger. This had a lot to do with the Fargo platform: slack touring geo, robust tubeset, and wider tires.

If my old Salsa ala Carte gets a “cotta” on the pasta cook scale, I’d say the Fargo 32” falls somewhere in between “al chiodo” and “al dente.” It feels stiff enough to carry weight without getting loopy but still more compliant than a Surly. Check out the Flex Capacitor for more info on the noodle scale.

Mechanical Concerns

From a mechanic’s point of view, there is something about the angle of the spokes and size of the cassette that makes for a very tight margin for adjusting the low limit without the cage of the derailleur hitting the spokes. I’ve had this happen on some 29er derailleur setups as well; the spoke’s attack angle is such that setting the low limit perfectly is imperative to keep the derailleur from ticking the spokes in the 52-tooth cog. This left me wondering if component manufacturers will have to be paying closer attention to how 32” wheels affect the setup of their drivetrain and brake systems. I was also curious if the bike would fit on my bike rack, and it did not. This is not a deal breaker for me, as my rack, the Kuat NV 2.0, probably wouldn’t fit a 20” wheeled bike either. This could be a concern if you use the bike for commuting and need one of the SportWerks-style racks to supplement your commute. Also, bigger wheels mean bigger boxes. So if you are traveling with this bike, you may need to be more careful when choosing a box or travel bag. Folks at Salsa have had success so far with Evoc bags traveling with their prototypes. These are small details to evaluate when adopting a new standard.

On The Necessity of 32″

Do we really need a new wheel size? Isn’t 29 inches plenty of inches? Honestly, I’m not totally sure. What I am sure of is that the Salsa Fargo Steel 32” is super comfy and looks great. And it harkens back to a Salsa that I know from the past. A Salsa that proclaims “If it ain’t moto, it’s worthless.” And that’s enough to sell me on it. I loved how it handled on the chunkiest of dirt roads, and I think that if you have the opportunity to try a 32”, you should, especially the Fargo. At the same time, I feel a bit like Carrie Bradshaw in reflecting on my experience of this bicycle. I have the desire to make a pun that will make you roll your eyes and shed a tear simultaneously. Maybe that’s because sometimes trends and new standards in cycling feel more like fashion than innovation.

Pros

  • Can’t beat the color; it’s beautiful
  • Frame is robust without feeling heavy
  • Plenty of mounting points to attach all the bags and racks
  • Better for taller riders
  • Insanely comfortable
  • You’ll make your friends wish they had the cool new thing

Cons

  • Maybe purple is not your thing (then you can just get the Ti one)
  • Might not fit in your car’s bike rack
  • You’ll need a bigger box to bring it on the plane
  • Somewhat less nimble in techy situations
  • Fewer options exist for tires and rims at this time

Spencer’s Take On The Fargo 32 Steel

While this is Sean’s review, we live in the same town, and I got to take the bike out for a few rides, so I wanted to add my thoughts and some details Joe Meiser of Salsa shared with me.

On the whole, I am excited by the prospect of a 32″ platform for us taller riders. Though the bike was sent with a negative rise stem, and since I’m dying on the “stack height is too low” hill, I swapped it out. In our moment of glory and comfort, the bike designers see fit to snatch victory from our hands with insane negative rise stems and short head tubes. Don’t let this become permissible.

I took the Fargo 32 out on some AZT singletrack as well as rough gravel roads that are quintessentially southern Arizona. At speed, the 32″ wheels do an impressive job of mediating chatter and holding tempo. On singletrack, I never found the bike overly unwieldy, even on tight switchbacks, though I wished it had flat bars more than once. At slow speeds, the large contact patch can feel sluggish, but I’m telling you, point this thing straight and it goooooes.

I found the overall silhouette of the new Fargo easier on the eyes, looking more akin to a gravel bike with its 80mm of suspension correction over the longer 100mm travel of the 29er Fargo. Despite the boost MTB spaced hubs, 73mm bottom bracket, and 2.4″ tires, the Fargo 32 always felt like a gravel bike to me. One could attribute this to my general lack of desire to ride drop bars on singletrack and my love for mountain bike-sized tires on my gravel bikes.

That new silhouette is due to the updated geometry of the Fargo, bringing the Fargo 32 in line with what I would expect from a modern mountain bike: longer TT, steeper seat tube angle, and slacker head tube angle. It may not surprise you that this project started out as an update to the 29er Fargo, but the engineers (even one who rides a small frame) decided they enjoyed the 32″ wheels more and ran with the idea. The geometry comes close to the geometry of the Tributary that I was so fond of a few years ago and wished would be offered on a non-e-bike.

I can’t decide if it is frustrating to see brands reuse many year-old 29er suspension-corrected forks on their 32″ bike or if that fact is just efficient and fine. The fork on the Fargo 32 is the now-discontinued Whisky No9 Boost LT fork. Joe from Salsa illuminated the fact that the fork allowed for ~80mm of suspension correction, which is the travel a few manufacturers have teased for 32″ forks. I was initially turned off by the mix of post mount and flat mount on either part of the bike, but Joe talked some sense into me. He mentioned that the post-mount fork is easily adaptable to flat mount, and I remembered most bikes need some kind of adapter for the brakes. The flat mount rear alternator dropout can also be swapped to post mount, if someone wanted to do a full post mount setup for flat bars, since this is a frameset after all. Bike manufacturers might not need to fully reinvent the wheel for new 32″ bikes, but I look forward to seeing where the numbers all land for the new forks, rigid and suspension.

I also inquired about the redesign for the Fargo 32, asking if a new tubeset had been selected for the bike. Joe told me that in addition to a specific new tubeset, the Fargo 32 Steel would be produced by the same premium factory as their Titanium offering.

Check out both the Ti and steel versions of the Fargo 32 over at Salsa Cycles.

author: spencer harding
